===============================================================================
RESIDENTIAL DWELLING INSURANCE
GENERAL POLICY CONDITIONS - PROPERTY DAMAGE COVER
Policy wording "WD-2026" - Buildings, Contents and Forcible Removal Edition
Fictional mock document created for test purposes only. All wording is
invented. No real contract.
===============================================================================

These conditions apply together with the General Contract Provisions and with
the Schedule, both of which form part of this contract. Sums insured, limits,
sub-limits, deductibles, periods and percentages shown in square brackets are
those stated in the Schedule.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 1 - PURPOSE AND KEY CONCEPTS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 What this insurance does

Combined residential insurance protects the policyholder against the financial
consequences of physical damage to their building and, where so agreed, against
the loss of the movable property kept in it. The perils that can be insured are
the ones bundled together in these conditions - fire, escape of water, storm and
hail, further natural hazards, and the forcible removal of insured property from
the insured location among them. Which of the insurable perils are actually
covered is agreed between insurer and policyholder and recorded in the schedule.

Where insured property is destroyed, damaged or removed, the insurer indemnifies
the cost of putting matters back. For the building the normal arrangement is
reinstatement in the same kind and quality, to a condition as new, on an
index-linked reinstatement basis with an enhancement. For movable insured
property the normal arrangement is replacement by an article of the same kind
and quality in new condition, within the sum insured for that property and
within any sub-limit that applies to the category concerned. A limited and
exhaustively listed range of consequential expenses triggered by a loss event -
debris removal, and the immediate securing of the insured location among them -
is also carried.

1.2 How the wording is to be read

Personal designations are to be understood as gender-neutral throughout; no
parallel male and female forms are used.

1.3 Explanation of recurring terms (not legally binding)

Policyholder - the insurer's contracting party and the purchaser of the cover.

Insured event - the event for which the insurer pays. An event is an insured
event only where it is one of the perils listed in Part 2, where it acts on
property that is insured under Part 4, and where that property was at the
insured location at the time.

Exclusion - a peril, a type of damage or an item of property for which no cover
exists. Exclusions delimit what has been promised and keep the cover
calculable. They appear in three places in these conditions: as general
exclusions applying across the contract, within the provisions on individual
perils and types of damage, and within the description of the insured property.

Sub-limit - a monetary ceiling applying to a defined category of insured
property, or to a single article within such a category, inside the sum insured
for that property. A sub-limit does not exclude the category; it caps what is
payable for it. Where a sub-limit is expressed per article, it is applied to
each article separately, and the balance of the loss on that article is borne by
the policyholder.

Schedule of specified articles - a list, attached to the contract and agreed
before the loss, in which individual articles of a high-value kind are named and
valued. An article that is not on such a list is an unspecified article and is
subject to the per-article sub-limit under 4.4.

Everyday movable property - movable property of the household kept for the
ordinary daily use of the occupants, which is neither of a high-value kind
within the meaning of 4.4 nor otherwise made subject to a sub-limit by the
schedule.

Index-linked reinstatement cover with enhancement - a basis of cover that works
from the amount that would have to be spent to rebuild in the same kind and
quality. Any additional cost caused by public-law restrictions on reinstatement
is picked up automatically. In addition, the level of cover is tracked against
movements in building costs; that tracking affects both the amount payable and
the premium.

Duties - the things the policyholder must do or refrain from doing before,
during and after an insured event. Observing safety requirements against fire,
frost or unauthorised access is an example. Breaching a duty puts the cover at
risk.

Secured lenders - creditors whose claim is secured by a charge registered
against the property. Their interests enjoy statutory protection: among other
things they must be brought into the process when insurance benefits are paid
out and when the contract is brought to an end.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 2 - INSURED PERILS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2.1 The perils that can be covered

The insurer indemnifies insured property that is destroyed or damaged by, or
lost or removed as a consequence of, the following events:

  (a) FIRE GROUP - fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning;
      explosion; deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft, its
      parts or its cargo; impact of a vehicle; scorching; smoke and soot.

  (b) ESCAPE OF WATER.

  (c) NATURAL HAZARDS, in two tiers:
        (c1) storm and hail;
        (c2) the further natural hazards - flood, backing-up of water,
             earthquake, ground subsidence, landslip, snow load, avalanche and
             volcanic eruption.

  (d) FORCIBLE REMOVAL OF INSURED PROPERTY from the insured location, as
      defined in 2.6.

2.2 How the groups combine

Each of the groups (a), (b), (c1) and (d) can be taken separately. The further
natural hazards under (c2) can only be taken in combination with one or more of
the perils in (a), (b) or (c1); they are not available on a standalone basis.
Group (d) can be taken for the building alone, or for the building together with
the movable insured property under 4.2.6.

2.3 The fire group defined

2.3.1 Fire
A fire is a combustion that has started without a hearth intended for it, or
that has escaped such a hearth, and that is capable of spreading under its own
power. Damage caused by a fire that developed out of a controlled, purposeful
fire is also covered.

2.3.2 Lightning strike
The direct passage of a lightning discharge onto property.

2.3.3 Overvoltage caused by lightning
Damage arising through overvoltage, overcurrent or short circuit, brought about
by a lightning discharge or by other atmospheric electricity, in insured
electrical installations and appliances.

2.3.4 Explosion and deflagration
Both are suddenly running force events resting on the tendency of gases or
vapours to expand. The two differ only in the intensity of that force.

An explosion of a vessel - a boiler, a pipe run and the like - is present only
under a further condition: the vessel wall must be torn open to such an extent
that a sudden equalisation of the pressure difference between the inside and
the outside occurs. Where an explosion inside a vessel is brought about by a
chemical reaction, tearing of the wall is not required.

2.3.5 Implosion
A sudden, unforeseen collapse of a hollow body under external overpressure
resulting from an internal underpressure.

2.3.6 Impact or crash of an aircraft
The impact or crash of an aircraft is covered, and equally the impact or crash
of its parts or its cargo.

2.3.7 Vehicle impact
The impact of a road, rail or water-borne vehicle against insured property is
covered, as is the impact of parts or cargo of such a vehicle. Consequential
damage to insured property arising from such an impact is covered.

Not covered is damage caused by a road or water-borne vehicle whose keeper or
driver is the policyholder or an occupant of the building.

Not covered is damage to means of transport of any kind, to their parts,
fittings and cargo, and to roads, drives and comparable trafficked surfaces.

2.3.8 Scorching
Scorch damage arising out of one of the events in 2.3.1 to 2.3.7 is covered.
Scorch damage from any other cause is covered up to [amount].

2.3.9 Smoke and soot
Smoke and soot damage arising out of one of the events in 2.3.1 to 2.3.8 is
covered.

Beyond that, damage is covered where smoke or soot directly damages or destroys
insured property, on condition that the smoke or soot escaped suddenly, and
contrary to intended operation, from a firing, heating, cooking or drying
installation situated on the insured site. Indemnity for this extension is
capped at [amount].

Not covered is damage arising from the gradual action of smoke or soot -
long-term surface soiling of the fogging type, for instance.

2.3.10 Damage excluded within the fire group
Not covered:
  (a) damage caused by earthquake, irrespective of any contributing causes;
  (b) damage to internal combustion engines caused by the explosions occurring
      inside the machine's combustion chamber, and damage arising at the
      switching elements of electrical switches through the gas pressure
      occurring inside them. Cover does exist, however, where such damage is
      the consequence of an insured fire event under 2.3.1.

2.4 Escape of water defined

2.4.1 The three headings
The escape of water peril covers three things: escape of water damage; fracture
damage to pipework inside buildings; and fracture damage to pipework outside
buildings.

2.4.2 Escape of water damage
Escaping water means water that has emerged contrary to its intended purpose
from:
  (a) pipes of the water supply, whether supply or drainage lines, or hoses
      connected to them;
  (b) other installations connected to those pipes or hoses, or the
      water-carrying parts of such installations;
  (c) heating or air-conditioning systems;
  (d) water-based extinguishing or sprinkler systems;
  (e) water beds or aquaria.

Operating fluids from heating or air-conditioning systems, and steam, also
count as escaping water. Fluids intended for the generation of energy do not.

Damage is also covered where it is caused by water that emerged, contrary to
its intended purpose, from rainwater drainage pipes running inside the
building. For this extension the exclusion of damage caused by precipitation
(see 3.3(c)) does not apply.

2.4.3 Fracture damage to pipework inside buildings
Covered inside buildings:

  (a) frost-related and other fracture damage to pipes of
        - the water supply, whether supply or drainage lines, and the gas
          supply, or hoses connected to them;
        - heating or air-conditioning systems;
        - water-based extinguishing or sprinkler systems;
        - rainwater drainage.
      This presupposes that the pipes concerned are not a structural component
      of a boiler, a water heater or a comparable installation.

  (b) frost-related fracture damage to the following installations:
        - bath and shower fittings, washbasins, lavatories, taps and valves
          together with their connection hoses;
        - radiators, boilers, water heaters and comparable parts of heating or
          air-conditioning systems.

The whole structural body of the building, including the floor slab, counts as
"inside the building". Pipes of a solar heating installation on the roof count
as pipes inside the building. Unless something else has been agreed, pipes and
installations beneath the floor slab are not insured, whether load-bearing or
not.

2.4.4 Fracture damage to pipework outside buildings
Covered outside buildings: frost-related and other fracture damage to supply
pipes of the water supply, or to pipes of heating or air-conditioning systems,
in each case insofar as the policyholder bears the risk for those pipes and
insofar as they either
  (a) serve the supply of insured buildings or installations, or
  (b) are situated on the insured site.

Indemnity for fracture damage to supply pipes that do not serve the supply of
insured buildings or installations is limited per insured event to the amount
agreed for that purpose.

Indemnity for fracture damage to supply pipes that are not situated on the
insured site is limited per insured event to the amount agreed for that
purpose.

2.5 Natural hazards defined

2.5.1 Storm
Storm means a weather-driven movement of air reaching at least the gale
threshold on the recognised scale of wind strength, expressed as a defined
minimum sustained wind speed.

Where the wind strength at the loss location cannot be established, storm is
presumed if the policyholder demonstrates either of the following:
  (a) in the vicinity of the insured site the air movement caused damage to
      buildings that were in sound condition, or to other property of
      comparable resistance; or
  (b) given the sound condition of the insured building - or of the building in
      which the insured property was located - the damage can only have arisen
      through storm. This applies equally to buildings structurally joined to
      the insured building.

2.5.2 Hail
Hail means solid precipitation in the form of grains of ice.

2.5.3 Which storm and hail events are covered
Only damage arising in one of the following ways is covered:
  (a) storm or hail acts directly on insured property, or on buildings in which
      insured property is located; consequential damage to insured property
      arising from this is covered;
  (b) storm or hail acts directly on buildings structurally joined to the
      insured building;
  (c) storm or hail acts directly on buildings structurally joined to buildings
      in which insured property is located;
  (d) storm or hail throws building parts, trees or other objects onto insured
      property, or onto buildings in which insured property is located;
      consequential damage to insured property arising from this is covered;
  (e) storm or hail throws building parts, trees or other objects onto
      buildings structurally joined to the insured building;
  (f) storm or hail throws building parts, trees or other objects onto
      buildings structurally joined to buildings in which insured property is
      located.

2.5.4 The further natural hazards

Flood
Flood means the inundation of the ground and soil of the insured site, or of
directly adjoining land, roads, footpaths or cycle paths, with substantial
quantities of surface water. It counts only where the inundation was caused by
  (a) the overflow of surface waters, standing or flowing,
  (b) precipitation, or
  (c) the emergence of groundwater at the surface as a consequence of (a) or
      (b).

Backing-up of water
Backing-up is present where water enters the building from the building's own
drainage pipes or from installations connected to them. It counts only where
the backing-up was caused by the overflow of surface waters, standing or
flowing, or by precipitation.

Earthquake
Earthquake means a naturally caused tremor of the ground triggered by
geophysical processes within the earth's interior.

Earthquake is presumed if the policyholder demonstrates either of the
following:
  (a) in the vicinity of the insured location the naturally caused ground
      tremor caused damage to buildings that were in sound condition, or to
      other property of comparable resistance; or
  (b) given the sound condition of the insured property, the damage can only
      have arisen through an earthquake.

Ground subsidence
A naturally caused sinking of the ground above naturally formed cavities.

Landslip
A naturally caused sliding or falling away of masses of earth or rock.

Snow load
The effect of the weight of masses of snow or ice. Snow or ice masses sliding
off roofs also count as snow load.

Avalanche
Masses of snow or ice descending a mountain slope.

Volcanic eruption
A sudden release of pressure on the rupturing of the earth's crust, accompanied
by flows of lava, eruptions of ash, or the escape of other materials and gases.

2.6 Forcible removal of insured property defined

2.6.1 The peril
The insurer indemnifies insured property that a third party takes away from the
insured location, or destroys or damages there, having gained access to the
enclosed part of the insured location
  (a) by breaking open, forcing, destroying or overcoming a closure element of
      the building - a door, a window, a shutter, a lock or a comparable
      barrier; or
  (b) by any other means involving the application of physical force to the
      building or to one of its closure elements.

2.6.2 Damage to the fabric caused by the access
Destruction of, or damage to, the insured building and its components brought
about in the course of gaining or attempting to gain such access is covered
under this peril. This applies whether or not any property was in fact taken
away. It extends to the closure elements themselves and to their locking and
securing mechanisms.

2.6.3 Loss of movable property
Where the movable property described in 4.2.6 is co-insured, the removal of that
property in the circumstances of 2.6.1 is covered. Indemnity follows Part 4 as to
which property is insured, and Part 7 as to amount, including the per-article and
per-event sub-limits under 4.4.

2.6.4 What does not count
Taking away without any application of physical force to the building or its
closure elements is not covered; nor is a removal effected by a person living in
the household of the policyholder, or by a person to whom access was entrusted.

2.6.5 Proof
The peril is presumed where traces of forced access on the building or its
closure elements are established by inspection, by photographic record or by an
official report taken at or shortly after the time of the loss, and the property
claimed as removed is itemised in accordance with 9.5.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 3 - EXCLUSIONS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3.1 General exclusions

3.1.1 War
Damage caused by war, warlike events, civil war, revolution, rebellion or
insurrection is not covered. This applies irrespective of any contributing
causes.

3.1.2 Civil commotion
Damage caused by internal civil unrest is not covered. This applies
irrespective of any contributing causes.

3.1.3 Nuclear energy
Damage caused by nuclear energy, nuclear radiation or radioactive substances is
not covered. This applies irrespective of any contributing causes.

3.1.4 Property that is not insured property
No indemnity is payable in respect of an object that is not insured property
under Part 4, or that was not at the insured location at the time of the event.
This applies however the loss is described and however it is invoiced.

3.2 Exclusions within the fire group

See 2.3.10.

3.3 Exclusions within the escape of water peril

Damage caused by the following is not covered, irrespective of any contributing
causes except where such causes are named below:
  (a) splash water or cleaning water;
  (b) dry rot and house-rot fungi of every kind;
  (c) groundwater, standing or flowing surface water, flood, precipitation, or
      a backing-up of water brought about by any of these causes;
  (d) earthquake, snow load, avalanche, volcanic eruption;
  (e) ground subsidence or landslip - unless escaping water within the meaning
      of 2.4.2 caused the subsidence or the landslip;
  (f) fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning; explosion;
      deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft; vehicle impact;
      scorching; smoke and soot damage;
  (g) the opening of sprinklers or the operation of sprinkler nozzles on
      account of a fire, on account of pressure testing, or on account of
      alteration or repair work to the insured building or to the extinguishing
      or sprinkler system;
  (h) storm, hail.

Damage to buildings or parts of buildings that are not ready for occupation is
not covered. The same applies to property located in such buildings or parts of
buildings.

3.4 Exclusions within the natural hazards

Damage caused by the following is not covered, irrespective of any contributing
causes except where such causes are named below:
  (a) storm surge;
  (b) the penetration of rain, hail, snow or dirt through windows, external
      doors or other openings that were not properly closed. This exclusion
      does not apply where those openings were created by storm or hail and
      constitute damage to the building;
  (c) groundwater, except insofar as it emerged at the surface as a result of
      precipitation or of the overflow of surface waters;
  (d) fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning; explosion;
      deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft; vehicle impact;
      scorching; smoke and soot damage. This exclusion does not apply insofar
      as those perils were triggered by an insured earthquake;
  (e) drought or desiccation.

Damage to buildings and parts of buildings that are not ready for occupation,
and to property located within them, is not covered. Damage to shop windows and
display windows is likewise not covered.

3.5 Exclusions within the forcible removal peril

Not covered, irrespective of any contributing causes:
  (a) loss established only as an unexplained shortage, disappearance or
      inventory difference, without traces of forced access within the meaning
      of 2.6.5;
  (b) loss of property while it is away from the insured location, including
      while it is being carried by a person or is contained in or on a means of
      transport, wherever that means of transport may be;
  (c) loss of banknotes, coin, bearer instruments, precious metal in bulk form
      and comparable monetary assets, save within the separate sub-limit agreed
      for them, where any;
  (d) loss caused or facilitated by the policyholder or by a person living in
      the household, and loss of property entrusted to a third party away from
      the insured location.

The sub-limits under 4.4 are not exclusions. Property to which a sub-limit
applies is insured property; indemnity for it is capped in accordance with that
sub-limit and the balance is borne by the policyholder.

3.6 Work beyond the affected parts, and outlay that is not a repair cost

Work carried out beyond those parts of the insured property that were themselves
affected by the insured event is not covered. Outlay that does not constitute a
repair cost is not indemnified. The delimitation in each case is governed by
7.1.5 to 7.1.9.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 4 - INSURED PROPERTY, INSURED LOCATION, SUB-LIMITS, DEDUCTIBLES
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

4.1 What is insured

Insured property comprises:
  (a) the buildings identified in the schedule;
  (b) their building components, including the closure elements of the building
      and their locking and securing mechanisms;
  (c) their building accessories;
  (d) terraces on the insured site that directly adjoin the building;
  (e) further site installations;
  (f) where so agreed in the schedule, the movable property of the household
      described in 4.2.6.

4.2 The categories defined

4.2.1 Building and dwelling
Buildings are structures connected to the ground. They must be capable of
affording protection against external influences and, for the purposes of these
conditions, must be intended for predominantly residential use.

Where the insured property is a self-contained dwelling within such a building,
these conditions apply to that dwelling and to those parts of the building that
constitute the policyholder's separate property, together with the
policyholder's share in the common parts.

4.2.2 Building components
Building components are items incorporated into a building that have lost their
independence through their firm connection with it. Fitted furniture and fitted
kitchens fall within this category where they were made individually for the
building and adapted to it with substantial installation effort. Add-on
furniture and add-on kitchens that are series-produced do not.

Also counting as building components are the fitting-out elements of the
dwelling: floor coverings together with their bedding, adhesive, underlay,
insulating and levelling layers; wall and ceiling finishes; interior and
external doors, windows and their frames; the closure, locking and securing
mechanisms fitted to them; and fixed trim, beading and comparable edging
elements.

4.2.3 Building accessories
Building accessories are movable items located inside the building or attached
to its exterior. They must serve the upkeep of the insured building or its
predominant intended purpose.

4.2.4 Terraces
Terraces are paved surfaces intended for occupation in the open air.

4.2.5 Further site installations
Further site installations means the items firmly connected with the ground and
soil of the insured site that are specified for that purpose in the schedule.

4.2.6 Movable property of the household
Where the schedule so provides, insured property also comprises the movable
property that the policyholder or the occupants keep at the insured location for
their private use and personal needs. This includes furnishings and equipment of
the household, articles of personal apparel and personal use of everyday
character, and articles of a high-value kind within the meaning of 4.4.

Movable property of the household is insured within the sum insured agreed for
it and, where a category sub-limit or a per-article sub-limit applies under 4.4,
within that sub-limit as well.

4.3 Property not insured

Not insured:
  (a) photovoltaic installations and their components - solar modules, mounting
      frames, fastening elements, inverters, module optimisers and the cabling.
      This extends to an electricity storage installation permanently connected
      to the photovoltaic installation and serving the supply of the building;
  (b) all items subsequently incorporated into the building by a tenant or by a
      condominium owner where that person both
        - procured or took the items over at their own expense, and
        - bears the risk for them.
      Where items are merely exchanged, the newly incorporated items are
      insured. Any different arrangement as to who bears the risk must be
      evidenced by the policyholder;
  (c) electronically stored data and programs. Costs of restoring
      electronically stored data and programs are covered only where this has
      been additionally agreed in the contract;
  (d) means of transport of every kind, together with their parts, fittings,
      accessories and cargo;
  (e) property of any description while it is situated away from the insured
      location.

4.4 Sub-limits for articles of a high-value kind

4.4.1 Articles of a high-value kind means articles of personal adornment and
comparable small articles made of, or set with, precious materials, together with
timepieces of corresponding character. Such articles are insured property under
4.2.6; the following ceilings apply to what is payable for them.

4.4.2 An article of a high-value kind that is not named and valued in a schedule
of specified articles agreed before the loss is an unspecified article.
Indemnity for each unspecified article is limited to [amount] per article,
irrespective of the value the article actually had. Where several such articles
are lost on the same occasion, the ceiling is applied to each article
separately; it is not an allowance that may be pooled or transferred between
them.

4.4.3 Indemnity for all unspecified articles of a high-value kind taken together
is limited to [amount], or to [percentage] of the sum insured for movable
property of the household, per insured event, whichever the schedule states.

4.4.4 Where an article is named and valued in a schedule of specified articles
agreed before the loss, indemnity for it is determined by the value stated there
and the per-article ceiling in 4.4.2 does not apply to it. The absence of such a
schedule, or the absence of the particular article from it, means that 4.4.2
applies to that article regardless of any evidence of its actual value produced
after the loss.

4.4.5 Articles of everyday character - modest pieces of personal adornment worn
in ordinary daily use whose individual value does not exceed the ceiling in
4.4.2 - are not affected by 4.4.2. They are indemnified in full under 7.1.1(d)
within the sum insured for movable property of the household.

4.4.6 Articles of personal apparel and other articles of personal use of everyday
character are not articles of a high-value kind. No per-article ceiling applies
to them. They are indemnified in full under 7.1.1(d) within the sum insured for
movable property of the household.

4.5 The insured location

The insured location is the insured site: the land parcel or parcels on which
the insured building stands. Where several buildings stand on one parcel, the
insured location is that part of the parcel which, by fencing or other
demarcation, belongs exclusively to the insured building or buildings. Movable
insured property is covered while it is inside the enclosed part of the insured
location.

4.6 Condominium and part-ownership units

4.6.1 Where the contract is with an association of condominium owners: if the
insurer is wholly or partly released from liability on account of the conduct of
individual condominium owners, it remains obliged to pay the remaining owners.
This applies to their separate property and to their shares in the common
property.

4.6.2 The co-ownership share of the owner against whom the insurer is wholly or
partly released is not indemnified, or is indemnified only in part.

The remaining condominium owners may nevertheless claim indemnity for that
co-ownership share. This presupposes that the additional indemnity is applied to
reinstating the common property. The condominium owner against whom the insurer
is wholly or partly released must reimburse the insurer for that additional
indemnity.

4.6.3 The two provisions above apply correspondingly to buildings insurance for
part-ownership units.

4.7 Deductibles

A deductible is the share of the indemnity, or the amount, that the policyholder
bears itself per insured event. Deductibles can be agreed individually. They may
differ from one insured peril and one insured benefit to another. Each is set
out in the schedule. A deductible is applied once per insured event to the
indemnity otherwise payable, after any sub-limit under 4.4 has been applied.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 5 - INSURED COSTS, LOSS OF RENT AND RENTAL VALUE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

5.1 Which costs are covered

The insurer reimburses the following costs where they were necessary as a
consequence of an insured event and were actually incurred:
  (a) debris removal and demolition costs;
  (b) costs of immediate securing and provisional protection of the insured
      location;
  (c) costs of moving and protecting property;
  (d) costs of lost water, gas and heating oil, and of electricity lost from
      storage installations;
  (e) hotel costs.

Reimbursement of each of these heads is limited to the amount agreed for it. The
list is exhaustive.

5.2 The cost heads defined

5.2.1 Debris removal and demolition
Costs incurred in clearing away and demolishing insured property. This includes
the expense of removing rubble and other remains of that property, transporting
them to the nearest disposal site, depositing them and destroying them.

5.2.2 Immediate securing and provisional protection
Where an insured event has left the building, or one of its closure elements,
open, unsecured or no longer capable of being closed and locked, the insurer
reimburses the measures reasonably taken without delay to restore a secure state.
This head comprises:
  (a) provisional closure of the opening - temporary boarding, sheeting, panels,
      props and comparable measures - together with their later removal;
  (b) attendance outside ordinary working hours where the state of the building
      did not permit the measure to be deferred;
  (c) restoration of the closure element concerned to a working and lockable
      condition, including the renewal of the locking and securing mechanism
      where the existing one was destroyed, damaged or rendered insecure by the
      event, and the making good of the frame and surrounding fabric disturbed
      in the process;
  (d) a temporary guarding or monitoring measure where no provisional closure
      could be achieved, for the period until it could be.

Renewal under (c) is on a like-for-like basis in accordance with 7.1.9. Where the
closure element or its mechanism is itself insured property under 4.2.2, the
policyholder may claim it either under this head or under Part 7, but not twice
in respect of the same insured event.

Indemnity under this head is capped at [amount] per insured event.

5.2.3 Moving and protecting property
Costs incurred in moving, altering or protecting other property, reimbursable
where those measures serve to reinstate or replace insured property.

5.2.4 Lost water, gas, heating oil and stored electricity
Costs arising because water, gas or heating oil escaped contrary to its intended
purpose as a result of an insured event. Additional wastewater charges fall
under this head. Costs of electricity lost from storage installations are also
reimbursed. Indemnity is capped at [amount] per insured event.

5.2.5 Hotel costs
Costs of accommodation in a hotel or similar, excluding incidentals such as
breakfast. The precondition is that the dwelling permanently occupied by the
policyholder has become uninhabitable and that confining themselves to a
habitable part of it cannot reasonably be expected of them.

Accommodation costs are reimbursed only where indemnity cannot be claimed under
another insurance contract.

Hotel or similar accommodation costs are reimbursed only to the extent that they
exceed the indemnity payable for rental value under 7.5.

Costs are reimbursed up to the point at which the dwelling is habitable again,
for a maximum of [number] days. Indemnity is capped at [amount] per day.

5.3 Loss of rent and rental value

The insurer reimburses:
  (a) loss of rent, where tenants of residential premises have lawfully stopped
      paying rent in whole or in part, or have terminated the tenancy, on
      account of an insured event. This includes the running service charges in
      the sense of tenancy law;
  (b) the locally customary rental value of residential premises occupied by the
      policyholder itself, including the running service charges in the sense of
      tenancy law. Reimbursement of rental value presupposes that, on account of
      the insured event, the policyholder cannot reasonably be expected to use at
      least parts of the dwelling;
  (c) any additional loss of rent under (a), or additional rental value under
      (b), caused by public-law restrictions on reinstatement.

5.4 The period for loss of rent and rental value

5.4.1 Loss of rent or rental value is reimbursed for the period during which the
rooms are unusable, but for no longer than [number] months from the occurrence
of the insured event.

5.4.2 Loss of rent or rental value is reimbursed only to the extent that the
policyholder has not culpably delayed the resumption of use where resumption was
possible. The provisions on the duty to avert and mitigate loss in the general
contract provisions apply.

5.5 Commercially used premises

For commercially used premises, insurance of loss of rent or of the locally
customary rental value can be agreed.

5.6 Optionally insurable extensions

5.6.1 Where the tenant terminates the tenancy on account of the insured event
and the policyholder is unable to re-let the dwelling after completion of the
works, the insurer also reimburses that loss of rent. This presupposes that the
policyholder was unable to let the rooms at the time reinstatement was completed
despite exercising the care required in commerce. It applies until the rooms are
re-let, and at most until the end of the period under 5.4.

5.6.2 Where a tenancy cannot be entered into on account of the insured event,
the insurer reimburses the loss of rent. This applies from the contractually
agreed start of the tenancy until the end of the period under 5.4. It
presupposes that the tenancy agreement had already been concluded at the time of
the insured event.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 6 - BASIS OF COVER AND PREMIUM
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

6.1 Insurable value

The insurable value forms the basis for calculating the indemnity.

The insurable value determined for the building applies equally to building
accessories, terraces and further site installations as defined in 4.2.3 to
4.2.5. For movable property of the household under 4.2.6 the insurable value is
the amount that would have to be spent to acquire property of the same kind and
quality in new condition, subject to the sums insured and sub-limits agreed.

6.2 Index-linked reinstatement value with enhancement

6.2.1 What is insured is the locally customary new-build value of the buildings
identified in the schedule, taken at the time of the insured event. Architects'
fees and other construction and planning costs form part of that value.

Where, within an insurance period, structural measures alter
  - the area,
  - the building type,
  - the construction, or
  - other agreed features underlying the premium calculation,
the following applies: cover subsists until the end of that insurance period,
even where the measure taken increases value.

6.2.2 Two elements are built into the index-linked reinstatement value with
enhancement:

  - Additional costs arising from public-law restrictions on reinstatement.
    These are the additional costs incurred because property affected by the
    loss cannot be reinstated or replaced in the same kind and quality on
    account of public-law requirements.

  - Price increases arising between the occurrence of the insured event and
    reinstatement initiated without delay.

6.2.3 The insurer tracks the cover under 6.2.1 against the development of
building costs (see 6.5). To that extent cover subsists on the basis of the
locally customary new-build value at the time of the reinstatement initiated
without delay after the insured event.

6.3 Index-linked current value with enhancement where reinstatement is omitted
    or delayed

For buildings that are not reinstated, or are reinstated late (see 7.6), only
the index-linked current value with enhancement is insured. That value is the
enhanced new-build value at the time of the insured event, less depreciation -
in particular depreciation for age and for the degree of wear.

6.4 Market value for permanently devalued buildings

For buildings designated for demolition, or otherwise permanently devalued, only
the achievable sale price excluding the land share is insured. Permanent
devaluation exists in particular where buildings can no longer be used for their
purpose.

6.5 How the premium is calculated

The bases for calculating the premium are:
  (a) the area;
  (b) the building type;
  (c) the construction and the fit-out;
  (d) the use;
  (e) the sum insured for movable property of the household and the sub-limits
      agreed under 4.4;
  (f) other agreed features material to the premium calculation; and
  (g) the adjustment factor.

The annual premium payable in each case is calculated by multiplying together:
  - the number of square metres of residential and usable floor area,
  - the premium per square metre of residential and usable floor area, and
  - the adjustment factor,
plus the premium element attributable to (e).

6.6 Adjustment of cover and premium

6.6.1 Where cover is adjusted under 6.2.3, the premium changes accordingly. That
happens when the adjustment factor rises or falls.

6.6.2 The adjustment factor changes with effect from 1 January of each year, for
the insurance period beginning in that year. It rises or falls in line with the
percentage by which the following two indices have moved:
  - a construction price index for residential buildings, taken for a defined
    reference month of the preceding year, and
  - a collectively agreed wage index for the construction sector, taken for a
    defined reference quarter of the preceding year.
Both indices are published by the competent national statistical authority.

In this adjustment the movement in the construction price index is weighted
[percentage] and the movement in the wage index [percentage].

When the year-on-year rates of movement are calculated, and again when the two
rates are weighted, the result is rounded to two decimal places at each step.

The adjustment factor is rounded to two decimal places.

In rounding, where the third decimal place is a five or higher the figure is
rounded up; otherwise it is rounded down.

6.7 Subsequent change in a premium-rating feature

6.7.1 Premium increase
Where a circumstance under 6.5(a) to (f) subsequently changes and a higher
premium results, the insurer may demand the higher premium from the point at
which the change is notified. A request to name and value an article in a
schedule of specified articles is a change of this kind and takes effect only
for the future.

6.7.2 Premium reduction
Where a circumstance under 6.5(a) to (f) subsequently ceases to apply and a
lower premium results, the insurer must reduce the premium from the point at
which it becomes aware of that. The same applies where such circumstances have
lost their significance, or where the policyholder had only mistakenly assumed
that they existed.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 7 - CALCULATION AND PAYMENT OF THE INDEMNITY
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

7.1 Basis of calculation

7.1.1 The insurer reimburses:

  (a) for destroyed buildings - the locally customary reinstatement costs under
      6.2.1, taken at the time of the insured event. This includes the
      additional costs under 6.2.2. Architects' fees and other construction and
      planning costs likewise form part of the indemnity.

  (b) for damaged buildings and other damaged insured property - the necessary
      repair costs at the time of the insured event. The insurer additionally
      compensates any diminution in value that the repair does not offset.
      Reimbursement is capped, however, at the insurable value at the time of
      the insured event.

  (c) for destroyed or lost other insured property - the replacement price for
      property of the same kind and quality in new condition, taken at the time
      of the insured event.

  (d) for movable property of the household under 4.2.6 that is destroyed, lost
      or removed - the amount required at the time of the insured event to
      acquire an article of the same kind, quality and standard in new
      condition. Where such an article is no longer obtainable, the amount
      required to acquire the nearest equivalent. Indemnity under this head is
      subject to the sum insured for that property and to any sub-limit under
      4.4.

7.1.2 Where technically still usable substance of the insured property may not
be used for reinstatement because of public-law requirements, the policyholder
receives corresponding indemnity under 7.1.1. This presupposes either
  (a) that the official orders in question were not issued before the insured
      event occurred, or
  (b) that use of the property was not, at the time of the insured event,
      wholly or partly prohibited on the basis of public-law requirements.

7.1.3 Price increases occurring between the insured event and reinstatement are
indemnified where reinstatement is secured within three years of the occurrence
of the insured event.

7.1.4 The achievable sale price of remains is set off in calculating the
indemnity under 7.1.1.

7.1.5 Extent of the repair
Indemnity is confined to those parts of the insured property that were
themselves affected by the insured event. The affected parts are the rooms,
surfaces, building components and items in which physical damage caused by the
event is established by the loss investigation - by inspection, by photographic
record, or by technical measurement taken at or shortly after the time of the
loss.

Work carried out in a room, on a surface, on a building component or on an item
that was not itself affected is not covered. This applies even where the work is
carried out
  (a) so that repaired and unrepaired parts correspond in appearance, colour,
      pattern, format or material;
  (b) for reasons of convenience, or because treating a whole room, surface or
      component is more economical than treating the affected part of it;
  (c) at the same time as covered work, in the course of it, or as part of the
      same overall project; or
  (d) by the same contractor as the covered work, and invoiced together with it.

Where a closure element and its mechanism were affected, the parts affected
include the mechanism, the element itself and so much of the frame and
surrounding fabric as had to be disturbed to restore a secure state.

7.1.6 Continuous surfaces
Where only part of a single continuous surface was affected, indemnity extends to
the cost of treating the adjoining unaffected sections of that same surface only
where a replacement material corresponding to the original is no longer
obtainable and a visible discontinuity would otherwise remain. It does not extend
to a separate room, nor to a surface, component or item that does not form part
of the same continuous affected surface.

7.1.7 Preparatory and ancillary work
The necessary repair costs under 7.1.1(b) include:
  (a) taking down, dismantling and disposing of the affected building components
      and finishes;
  (b) the drying, dehumidification and moisture-removal measures necessary before
      the repair can be carried out, and the necessary preparation of the
      substrate or supporting structure before a new finish is applied;
  (c) materials of a type, quality, grade and specification corresponding to
      those in place immediately before the insured event, including any bedding,
      adhesive, sealing, underlay, insulating or levelling layer that formed part
      of the component as installed before the loss;
  (d) unaffected trim, beading, edging and comparable finishing elements that have
      to be taken off in order to repair an affected component and that cannot be
      refitted afterwards.

7.1.8 Outlay that is not a repair cost
The following do not constitute repair costs and are not indemnified, however they
may be described or invoiced:
  (a) measures directed at the general condition, cleanliness, tidiness, upkeep,
      modernisation or improvement of the insured property, as distinct from
      making good the damage caused by the insured event. This does not affect
      the removal of debris and residues under 5.2.1, nor the securing measures
      under 5.2.2;
  (b) outlay belonging to a contractor's own business operation rather than to the
      repair - its own tools and consumable small equipment, its own diagnostic
      and measuring devices, provisioning for its own personnel, and general
      administrative, handling or processing charges levied in addition to
      itemised labour and materials;
  (c) the same item of cost where it is invoiced more than once in respect of the
      same insured event, whether by one contractor or across several trades;
      only the first such charge is indemnified;
  (d) an upgrade of a security or closure standard beyond the standard in place
      immediately before the insured event, to the extent of the upgrade.

7.1.9 No improvement on the pre-loss standard
Reinstatement proceeds on the basis of the type, quality, grade and specification
in place immediately before the insured event. Where a higher specification, a
larger format, a superior material or a premium range is chosen instead,
indemnity is limited to the cost of an equivalent standard-grade replacement
corresponding to what was in place before the loss; the difference is borne by
the policyholder.

7.1.10 Application of sub-limits
Where a sub-limit under 4.4 applies to an article, indemnity for that article is
calculated under 7.1.1(d) and then reduced to the sub-limit. The reduction
concerns that article alone. Other articles claimed on the same occasion, and
other heads of the claim, are unaffected by it and remain payable in full within
their own limits. Any per-event ceiling under 4.4.3 is applied after the
per-article ceilings and before the deductible.

7.2 Market value

Insofar as a building is designated for demolition or otherwise permanently
devalued, insured property is indemnified at the achievable sale price excluding
the land share.

7.3 Construction specification lower or higher than described

7.3.1 Where the insured buildings, in their actual construction specification at
the time of the insured event, are of lower value than described in the contract,
the following applies: the insurer is not obliged to compensate more than the
loss actually incurred, measured at the locally customary new-build value.

7.3.2 Where the actual construction specification at the time of the insured
event is of higher value, the following applies: this can lead to a reduction of
the indemnity. The basis for the indemnity is then the construction
specification described in the contract (see 6.5(a) to (f)). In that case the
insurer reimburses only the locally customary reinstatement costs (7.1.1(a)) or
the necessary repair costs (7.1.1(b)) for that specification.

The following provisions remain unaffected by this: the scope and adjustment of
cover (Part 6); breach of the pre-contractual duty of disclosure under the
general contract provisions; and increase in risk (9.3, and the corresponding
provisions of the general contract provisions).

7.4 Costs

Insured costs under Part 5 are reimbursed where it is demonstrated that they were
actually incurred. The indemnity limits agreed for each head are applied. A cost
falling outside the exhaustive list in 5.1 is not reimbursed.

7.5 Loss of rent and rental value

The insurer reimburses the insured loss of rent or rental value up to the end of
the agreed period under 5.4.

7.6 The reinstatement element of the indemnity

The policyholder acquires a claim to payment of that part of the indemnity which
exceeds the current-value loss - the reinstatement element - only on the
following conditions:
  (a) the policyholder ensures that it will use the indemnity to reinstate or
      replace insured property of the same kind and intended purpose at the
      previous location; and
  (b) the reinstatement or replacement is secured within three years of the
      occurrence of the insured event.

For movable property of the household, replacement within [number] months of the
insured event is sufficient.

Where reinstatement at the previous location is legally impossible or cannot be
justified economically, it is sufficient to erect the building at another
location within the same country.

The policyholder must repay the reinstatement element where, through its own
fault, the property was not reinstated or replaced within a reasonable period.

7.7 Value added tax

Value added tax is reimbursed only if and to the extent that it was actually
incurred on the occasion of the reinstatement or replacement. It is not
reimbursed where the policyholder is entitled to recover input tax.

7.8 Deductible

Deductibles are deducted from the indemnity in the amount agreed, once per
insured event.

7.9 When the indemnity falls due

7.9.1 The indemnity falls due once the insurer has conclusively determined the
claim as to its basis and its amount.

One month after notifying the loss, the policyholder may claim as an interim
payment the amount that is, on the prevailing assessment, payable as a minimum.

7.9.2 That part of the indemnity which goes beyond the current-value loss falls
due once the policyholder has demonstrated that it has secured the reinstatement
or replacement.

7.10 Repayment of the reinstatement element

The policyholder is obliged to repay indemnity paid under 7.9.2 where, through
its own fault, the property was not reinstated or replaced within a reasonable
period. This extends to any interest the insurer has paid under 7.11.2.

7.11 Interest

The following applies to interest, insofar as no more extensive obligation to pay
interest arises on another legal basis:

7.11.1 The indemnity bears interest from the notification of the loss. This does
not apply insofar as the indemnity was paid within one month.

7.11.2 That part of the indemnity which goes beyond the current-value loss bears
interest from the point at which the policyholder demonstrated that it has
secured the reinstatement or replacement.

7.11.3 The interest rate is [number] percentage point(s) below the applicable
statutory base rate of interest, but at least [percentage] and at most
[percentage] per year.

Interest falls due together with the indemnity.

7.12 Suspension of time limits

In calculating the periods under 7.9, 7.11.1 and 7.11.2, any period during which
the indemnity cannot be determined or cannot be paid owing to the fault of the
policyholder is left out of account.

7.13 Deferral of payment

The insurer may defer payment for as long as:
  (a) there is doubt as to the policyholder's entitlement to receive payment;
  (b) official or criminal proceedings against the policyholder or its
      representative arising out of this insured event are still pending;
  (c) a legally required involvement of a secured lender has not taken place.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 8 - EXPERT DETERMINATION PROCEDURE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

8.1 Determining the amount of the loss

After an insured event has occurred, the policyholder may require that the amount
of the loss be determined in an expert determination procedure.

Insurer and policyholder may also agree on such a procedure jointly.

8.2 Further determinations

Policyholder and insurer may agree to extend the expert determination procedure
to further determinations relating to the insured event. The procedure concerns
the amount of the loss. It does not alter a sub-limit agreed under 4.4, and a
valuation obtained in the course of it does not convert an unspecified article
into a specified one.

8.3 Procedure before the determination

8.3.1 Each party is to nominate one expert in text form - by email, fax or letter,
for example. A party that has nominated its expert may call on the other party in
text form to nominate the second expert; in doing so it must name the expert it
has itself nominated. The second expert must be nominated within two weeks of
receipt of that request. If that does not happen, the requesting party may have
the expert appointed by the court with local jurisdiction for the loss location.
Where the insurer makes the request, it must draw the policyholder's attention to
this consequence.

8.3.2 The insurer may not nominate as expert:
  (a) competitors of the policyholder;
  (b) persons standing in a permanent business relationship with the
      policyholder;
  (c) persons employed by competitors or business partners of the policyholder,
      or standing in a comparable relationship with them.

8.3.3 Before beginning their determinations, the two experts nominate in text
form a third expert as umpire. The restriction in 8.3.2 applies to that
nomination as well. If the experts cannot agree, the umpire is appointed by the
court with local jurisdiction for the loss location, on the application of either
party.

8.4 Content of the determination

The experts' findings must state:
  (a) a schedule of the lost, the destroyed, the removed and the damaged insured
      property, together with the corresponding insurable values at the time of
      the insured event, itemised article by article where a per-article
      sub-limit may apply;
  (b) the reinstatement and replacement costs;
  (c) the residual values of the property affected by the loss;
  (d) the insured costs and the insured loss of rent or rental value.

8.5 Procedure after the determination

Each expert transmits its findings to both parties simultaneously. Where the two
sets of findings diverge, the insurer passes them to the umpire without delay.
The umpire decides the points that remain in dispute. In doing so, the experts'
findings form the limits of the umpire's scope for decision. The umpire transmits
its decision to both parties simultaneously.

The findings of the experts, or of the umpire, are binding on the contracting
parties. They are not binding where it is demonstrated that they manifestly
deviate substantially from the true state of affairs.

The insurer calculates the indemnity on the basis of binding findings.

Where the findings are not binding, the court makes a binding determination. The
same applies where the experts cannot or will not make the determination, or
where they delay it.

8.6 Costs

Unless something else has been agreed, each party bears the costs of its own
expert. The costs of the umpire are borne by the two parties in equal shares.

8.7 Duties remain unaffected

The expert determination procedure does not affect the policyholder's duties.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 9 - POLICYHOLDER DUTIES AND INCREASE IN RISK
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

9.1 Contractually agreed safety requirements before an insured event

The following safety requirements apply as contractually agreed additional
duties:

9.1.1 Insured property must be kept in proper condition at all times. This
applies in particular to water-carrying installations and equipment, to roofs,
to items attached to the exterior, and to the closure elements of the building
and their locking and securing mechanisms. Defects or damage to such property
must be remedied without delay.

9.1.2 Buildings or parts of buildings that are not in use must be inspected
sufficiently frequently at every time of year. In addition, all water-carrying
installations and equipment there must be shut off, drained, and kept drained.

9.1.3 During the cold season all buildings and parts of buildings must be heated,
and this must be checked sufficiently frequently. Alternatively, all
water-carrying installations and equipment there must be shut off, drained, and
kept drained.

9.1.4 To avoid flood and backing-up damage:
  (a) in rooms at risk of backing-up, backflow prevention devices must be kept
      operational;
  (b) the drainage lines on the insured site must be kept clear.

9.1.5 While the dwelling is unoccupied, the closure elements of the building must
be kept closed and locked in the manner for which they were designed.

9.2 Duties after an insured event

9.2.1 The policyholder must avert and mitigate the loss so far as it reasonably
can. Where an insured event has left the building or one of its closure elements
open or unsecured, taking measures without delay to restore a secure state is
part of that duty. Costs so incurred are reimbursed under 5.2.2 within the limit
agreed there, and the insurer may not decline them on the ground that they were
taken before the loss was inspected.

9.2.2 Where property has been removed by a third party, the policyholder must
notify the competent authority without delay and submit an itemised list of the
property concerned.

9.3 Consequences of a breach of duty

Where the policyholder breaches one of the duties in 9.1 or 9.2, the following
applies, subject to the conditions set out in the general contract provisions:
the insurer is entitled to terminate the contract. It may also be wholly or
partly released from liability.

9.4 Circumstances constituting an increase in risk

An increase in risk subject to notification under the general contract provisions
may exist in particular in the following cases:
  (a) a circumstance changes about which the insurer asked before the contract
      was concluded;
  (b) the building, or the predominant part of it, is no longer in use;
  (c) construction work is carried out on the building in the course of which the
      roof is wholly or partly removed;
  (d) construction work on the building renders it predominantly unusable;
  (e) a commercial operation is taken up or changed within the building;
  (f) the building is placed under heritage protection after conclusion of the
      contract;
  (g) an agreed security or closure standard is reduced or ceases to be
      maintained.

9.5 Consequences of an increase in risk

The consequences of an increase in risk are governed by the general contract
provisions.

9.6 Claims presentation

Each item claimed must be presented in such a way that it can be allocated to an
insured peril under Part 2, to insured property under Part 4, and to a head of
indemnity under Part 5 or Part 7. Where a per-article sub-limit under 4.4 may
apply, the claim must itemise each article separately - description, estimated
value, approximate age or date of acquisition - so that the ceiling can be
applied to each article on its own. An article presented only as part of an
undifferentiated group is treated as a single unspecified article for that
purpose.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 10 - CANCELLATION, SECURED LENDERS, TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

10.1 Cancellation where a security right has been registered

Where a secured lender has registered its charge over the property, cancellation
of the insurance relationship by the policyholder in respect of the fire peril
group - fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning; explosion;
deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft; vehicle impact;
scorching; smoke and soot damage - is effective only in the following cases:

10.1.1 the policyholder demonstrated, at least one month before expiry of the
insurance contract, that at the point in time at which the cancellation was at
the latest permissible the property was no longer encumbered with the charge; or

10.1.2 the policyholder demonstrated, at least one month before expiry of the
insurance contract, that the secured lender consented to the cancellation.

This does not apply to a cancellation following a disposal of the property, or to
a cancellation in the insured event.

10.2 Legal position following a transfer of ownership

10.2.1 Where the policyholder disposes of the insured property, the acquirer
steps into its place in the insurance contract. This happens at the time of the
transfer of ownership; in the case of real property, at the date of registration
in the land register. From that time the acquirer takes over the rights and
obligations of the policyholder under the insurance relationship.

10.2.2 Seller and acquirer are jointly and severally liable for the premium. This
applies to the premium for the insurance period in which the transfer of
ownership occurs.

10.2.3 The insurer need only recognise the acquirer's entry into the insurance
contract once it becomes aware of that entry.

10.3 Rights of cancellation on a transfer of ownership

10.3.1 The insurer is entitled to cancel the insurance contract as against the
acquirer, observing a notice period of one month. This right of cancellation
lapses if the insurer does not exercise it within one month of becoming aware of
the disposal.

10.3.2 The acquirer is entitled to cancel the insurance contract with immediate
effect, or with effect from the end of the current insurance period, in text form
- by email, fax or letter, for example. That right of cancellation lapses if the
acquirer does not exercise it within one month of the acquisition. Where the
acquirer is unaware that the insurance exists, the right of cancellation lapses
one month after the acquirer becomes aware of it.

10.3.3 In the event of a cancellation under 10.3.1 or 10.3.2, the seller alone
remains liable for payment of the premium.

10.4 Duties of notification

10.4.1 The disposal must be notified to the insurer without delay, in text form,
by the seller or by the acquirer.

10.4.2 Where that notification has been omitted, the insurer is not obliged to
pay in the insured event. This applies only where both of the following
conditions are met:
  - the insured event occurred later than one month after the point at which the
    notification ought to have been received by the insurer; and
  - the insurer demonstrates that it would not have concluded the existing
    contract with the acquirer.

10.4.3 By way of departure from 10.4.2, the insurer is obliged to pay in the
following cases:
  - it was aware of the disposal at the point in time at which the notification
    ought to have been received by it; or
  - at the time of the insured event the period for the insurer's cancellation
    had already expired and it had not cancelled.

END OF DOCUMENT

case.description:
Burglary at the insured home. The back door was forced during the day while the house was empty, and the intruders took clothing and personal effects along with some everyday jewellery.

The jewellery was modest - costume and everyday pieces, nothing especially valuable - and the clothing was ordinary wear. The police were called and gave a reference number.

A tradesperson re-secured the forced door afterwards. The whole thing was billed as a short couple of summary lines.
